Newsletter: One Painful Problem · Edition 1

Series 1 · Agent 5 | The year-end fixed asset review, done from the general ledger

Zac Lu, CPA, LSSBBFree, tested tools for accountants

In January, the bookkeeper at Ridgeline Landscaping sends over the year's books with a note: "We bought a new truck and a mower this year. Everything else is the same."

Last year's depreciation schedule has six assets on it. The new truck and the mower are in the Vehicles and Equipment accounts, where they belong. The rest of what the schedule needs is scattered through a hundred lines of general ledger:

  • a $6,900 shop door replaced, posted to Repairs and Maintenance;
  • a $5,600 trailer sprayer, posted to Small Tools;
  • $16,000 from selling the old F-250, deposited and credited straight to Vehicles, so no gain was ever recorded and the truck's depreciation is still on the books;
  • $16,800 of depreciation booked during the year, when this year's depreciation comes to $24,610.

Ridgeline is invented. It is the sample client for this tool. But every accountant who prepares year-end returns has met it. The depreciation schedule only knows what someone entered, and nobody tells you about the door.

Finding all of this by hand means reading every line of the fixed asset accounts, then filtering repairs, supplies and tools for big bills, then tying the opening balances to last year's schedule. For one client that is about an hour. Miss something and you skip a year of depreciation, expense a purchase that should be on the schedule, leave a gain off the return, or end up with books that no longer agree with it.

This is Series 1, Agent 5: a free tool that does the reading, so you can spend the time on the decisions.

What it gives you

You drop in the client's general ledger for the year, exported from QuickBooks Online, QuickBooks Desktop or Xero. You get a workpaper you can print or save as a PDF:

  • What to add to the depreciation schedule, with dates to confirm. For Ridgeline: the mower, the F-350, the door and the sprayer, $88,550.
  • What to take off. The F-250, with the gain worked out: $13,375.
  • The proposed entries, as numbered adjusting entries with debits and credits: reclassify the door and the sprayer, record the truck sale, bring depreciation up by $7,810.
  • The balances after those entries, to tie to the schedule's totals.
  • The questions for the client. When was each asset put into use? Is it new or used? For a vehicle: its gross vehicle weight rating, and the business-use percentage.
  • The roll-forward of cost and accumulated depreciation, tied to the books.

The file is read on your computer. Nothing is uploaded, stored or sent.

How it works: the page finds, you decide

The screen takes you through four steps. A bar at the top shows where you are, and each step says whether the page did it or you have to.

1. Give the ledger. Automatic. The page reads every account and checks that each one adds up to the report's own totals. If a line is missing, it stops and tells you to export the ledger again.

2. Check the accounts. You check. The page sorts the accounts by name: fixed assets, accumulated depreciation, depreciation expense, the expense accounts where purchases hide, and the rest. It recognizes QuickBooks' "Original cost" and "Depreciation" sub-accounts. It knows that "Truck Loan" and "Gain on Sale of Equipment" are not assets. If an account is wrong, you pick the right kind and everything is worked out again.

3. Decide what was found. You decide. This is where the hour goes, and where the tool helps most:

  • Purchases recorded as assets. Listed automatically, with flags when one needs a second look: a trade-in recorded at the net price, land (not depreciated), a journal entry, or loan payments posted to the asset account.
  • Bills in expense accounts that may be equipment. Every bill over $2,500 in repairs, supplies, tools, computer and auto accounts. The page decides none of them. You choose capitalize or keep as expense. The screen reminds you that the de minimis safe harbor is per invoice or per item, so Ridgeline's two laptops and a dock, $3,480 on one bill, can stay expensed. A quarterly service contract is marked as one.
  • Credits to asset accounts. Sorted into returns, sales already booked properly, and money received for an asset that was posted straight to the asset. For those, you type the asset's cost and depreciation from the schedules, and the page works out the gain or loss and the entry.
  • Does it agree? Type last year's schedule totals and this year's depreciation. The page compares them with the books.

4. Print the workpaper. Built from your choices. Anything still undecided is listed at the top in red, and left out until you decide it.

Before release, a separate AI review played a skeptical CPA. It found nine ways the first version gave wrong answers. It counted loan payments as purchases. It proposed reclassing a forklift that had already been reclassed. It treated a properly booked sale as unrecorded. It pre-ticked purchases as capital. All are fixed, and each is now one of the 22 test files the tool must pass, 758 checks in all. Two more reviews played a first-time user, working from the screen alone. After the first, the tool was rebuilt around its four steps. After the second, it got a workpaper you can file: journal entries, the balances after them, and a reason for each decision.

Build it yourself

You don't need to download anything from me to have this tool. It comes from one prompt, and you can rebuild it with an AI assistant in about 15 minutes. You need no coding and no Excel skills.

What you need

  • A computer with a web browser and an internet connection. The page you build loads its spreadsheet reader from the internet each time it opens. (The ready-made tool in the repository works offline.)
  • An AI chat assistant that can write a long piece of code in one reply, such as Claude at claude.ai. The reply is long (about 1,000 lines), so a free plan may stop partway; a paid plan is safer.
  • About 15 minutes, most of it waiting for the reply.

Steps

  1. Copy the prompt. The safest copy is the master on GitHub. The repository's name is a single hyphen, so the address ends in "/-", and that is right. Open PROMPT.txt and press the "Copy raw file" button (two small squares, top right of the file). It is also printed in full below.
  2. Paste it into a new chat in your AI assistant and send it.
  3. Wait for one long block of code. If the assistant offers it as a file to download, or shows it in a side panel with a download or copy button, use that. If the reply stops partway, write: "Please send the complete file again in one code block."
  4. Save it as a web page. If there was no download, copy the whole code block into a plain-text editor and save it as what-goes-on-the-asset-schedule.html. On Windows, use Notepad: in the Save dialog, set "Save as type" to "All files", or it saves as .html.txt. On a Mac, use TextEdit: first choose Format, then Make Plain Text, and when it asks, choose "Use .html".
  5. Open it. Double-click the file. You should see "What goes on the asset schedule?" and a box to drop a file into.
  6. Try it on the sample client before any real file. Download the Ridgeline Landscaping ledger, last year's schedule and this year's depreciation report. On each page, press "Download raw file". Drop the ledger in and follow the steps on the screen.

What you should see. The top line reads "Ridgeline Landscaping LLC: $76,050.00 recorded as assets this year; $26,980.00 more found in expense accounts for you to decide; 1 sale or write-off to settle." In step 2, press "The accounts are right". In step 3b, capitalize the door and the sprayer (to Equipment, the default; the reason is optional) and keep the rest as expenses. For the old truck in 3c, type its $42,000.00 cost and $36,750.00 of depreciation at the end of last year, from last year's schedule, and $2,625.00 for this year, from this year's report. In step 3d, type the Total rows of the two schedules, 210,900.00 and 97,350.00, and this year's total, 24,610.00, then press Compare. The top line then reads "Ridgeline Landscaping LLC: $88,550.00 to add to the depreciation schedule; 1 asset to take off." The workpaper shows a gain of $13,375.00 and four adjusting entries, the last one $7,810.00 of depreciation. The full walkthrough is in the sample's README.

If it does not work

  • A blank page, or half a page: the code was cut off. Ask the assistant for the complete file again.
  • Nothing happens when you drop the file: the page could not load its spreadsheet reader. Check your internet connection; a company firewall can block it. Or use the ready-made tool.
  • A box forgets what you typed when you move to the next one: tell the assistant exactly that, and ask it to keep what you type in every box and to work the figures out only when you press the button.
  • Different numbers: tell the assistant what you expected, quoting the line above, and ask it to fix the file so it follows the prompt exactly.
  • Still stuck: the ready-made, tested tool is in the repository. It is one file that works offline.

The repository. The One Painful Problem repository on GitHub holds everything for this tool:

  • a README with these same steps;
  • the master prompt;
  • the sample client and what you should see;
  • the ready-made tool;
  • the 22 test files and their results.

Use it as the master copy if anything below looks wrong.

The prompt. Copy it from the master copy on GitHub if you can. LinkedIn can change quotes and line breaks.

Build me a complete, working tool as ONE self-contained HTML file named what-goes-on-the-asset-schedule.html. Reply with the whole file in a single code block, with nothing left out or shortened, so I can save it and open it in my browser.

WHO IT IS FOR AND WHAT IT DOES
It is for a US accountant at year end. She is expert in accounting, not technical, and works on a desktop. She gives it a client's general ledger for the year, exported to Excel or CSV from QuickBooks Online, QuickBooks Desktop or Xero. The page lists what the depreciation schedule and the year-end entries need: purchases recorded as fixed assets, bills in expense accounts that may be equipment, assets sold or written off, and whether the books agree with last year's depreciation schedule and this year's depreciation. The page finds; she decides. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is uploaded. All money is whole cents (integers), debit positive, worked out in code.

TECHNICAL BASICS
- Load the spreadsheet reader with: <script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/xlsx/0.18.5/xlsx.full.min.js"></script>
- Read the file with XLSX.read: .csv or .txt as text with {type:"string", raw:true}; anything else as {type:"array"}. Use the sheet with the most rows, via XLSX.utils.sheet_to_json(sheet, {header:1, raw:true, defval:null, blankrows:true}).
- Refuse a .pdf at once (window.__report stays unset) ("... is a PDF. Export the general ledger to Excel or CSV and drop that."), and any extension other than xlsx, xlsm, xls, csv, txt.
- Set window.__report to the report object (listed at the end) every time the review is produced or redone, without fields whose names start with "_". Set it to undefined when a new file starts loading. If anything throws, show the error and set window.__report = {status:"ERROR", message}.
- Large type (18px or more), plain words, high contrast, light background. Works on a phone: on narrow screens every table becomes stacked cards, each cell labelled with its column name. Print styles: see step 4.

READING NUMBERS AND DATES
- An amount is a number (cents = round(n*100)) or text like 1,234.56, $1,234.56, (1,234.56), -1,234.56 or 1,234.56- . Parentheses or a minus make it negative; $, commas and spaces are ignored. Blank, "-", en dash or em dash is no amount.
- A date becomes a day number. Accept: an Excel serial number between 20000 and 80000 (day = n - 25569); YYYY-MM-DD; M/D/YYYY or M/D/YY (US order, two-digit years are 20YY); "15 Mar 2026" or "15-Mar-2026"; "March 15, 2026" or "Mar. 15 2026".
- Show dates on screen as M/D/YYYY and money as $1,234.56. In window.__report, every date is "YYYY-MM-DD" and money is dollars as a number.

READING THE GENERAL LEDGER
1. Heading row: the first of the first 20 rows whose cells (lower case, trimmed) include "date", and "amount" (or both "debit" and "credit"), and "balance" or "running balance". Columns: date = "date"; type = "transaction type", else "type", else "source"; num = "num", else "reference", else "ref", else "no."; name = "name", else "contact"; memo = "memo/description", else "memo", else "description"; amount; debit; credit; balance = "balance", else "running balance". Layout: Xero if there is "running balance"; else QuickBooks Online if there is "amount"; else QuickBooks Desktop.
2. Title lines are the rows above the heading row, each row's non-empty cells joined by spaces. If there is no heading row: status NOT_RECOGNIZED, with a message naming what it is when the title lines say trial balance, profit and loss (or income statement), balance sheet, or aging/aged: "This is a trial balance, not a general ledger. I need the general ledger for the year: every transaction, grouped by account, with a Date column, an Amount column (or Debit and Credit), and a Balance column."
3. Rows below the heading row, in order (skip blank rows). Keep a stack of open accounts:
   - A row with a cell "Beginning Balance" or "Opening Balance": the account on top of the stack gets its opening balance from the balance column.
   - A row with a cell "Closing Balance": the account closed last gets its closing balance from the balance column.
   - A row whose first non-empty cell starts with "Total" (any case): if it is exactly "Total" (any case: the grand total), ignore it. Otherwise it closes the account on top of the stack (pop it): store its total (the amount column, or debit minus credit) and, if the balance cell has an amount, its total balance.
   - A row with a readable date in the date column: a line of the account on top of the stack, with date, type, num, name, memo and amount (amount column, or debit minus credit). If the balance cell has an amount, keep it as the account's last balance (a blank cell changes nothing). If no account is open, the row is unread.
   - A row with an amount (in the amount, debit or credit column; the balance column does not count) but no readable date: unread (keep its row number).
   - Any other row: an account header. Its label is the first non-empty cell, cleaned: remove a trailing code in parentheses of up to 10 letters, digits, dots or hyphens, like " (710)"; remove a leading account number like "15000 · " or "1520 " or "1520 - ". Its opening balance is the balance cell if it has an amount (QuickBooks Desktop puts it there), else 0. If an account is open on the stack, the new one is its sub-account: its full name is "Parent:Child". Push it on the stack.
   - Every account's ending = opening + the sum of its lines. Keep only accounts with lines or a non-zero opening.
4. The file adds up: for each account header read (including parents with no lines of their own), in file order, take it together with all its sub-accounts. It does not add up if its total is not the sum of all their lines, or its total balance is not the sum of all their endings, or its own closing balance or last balance is not its own ending. List those accounts.
5. Period, from the title lines: "January 1 - December 31, 2026" or "July 1, 2025 - June 30, 2026" (if the first year is missing, it is the second year, or the year before when the first month is later than the second); "1 January 2026 to 31 December 2026"; "January - December 2026" (first day of the first month to last day of the second). The words between may be -, en dash, to or through. None found: period unknown.
6. Company: the first title line that does not contain "general ledger", "account transactions", "transaction detail", "basis", "period" or a four-digit year.

WHAT EACH ACCOUNT IS (its role)
Work on the cleaned full name in lower case. For a sub-account "Parent:Child" (the parent's role here is the one worked out from its name, not one chosen on screen): if the child contains "depreciation" and the parent's role is fixed asset, it is accumulated depreciation; otherwise use the child's own role, but if that is "other" and the parent's role is fixed asset, it is a fixed asset. For one name, the first match wins:
- "accumulated amortization" or "accum amort" (with or without a dot after accum): other.
- "accumulated depreciation" or "accum depr" (with or without the dot): accumulated depreciation.
- contains "depreciation": depreciation expense.
- contains "amortization": other.
- fixed asset (cost): contains equipment, furniture, fixture(s), vehicle(s), truck(s), trailer(s), machinery, computer(s), leasehold improvement(s), "improvements", building(s), the word "land", "fixed asset(s)" or "property and equipment"; AND contains none of: expense(s), rental, the word "rent", repair(s), maintenance, small, supplies, the word "lease" (but "leasehold" is fine), fuel, insurance, registration, software, internet, minor, the words loan(s) or note(s), payable, interest, words starting gain, loss or sale, income, revenue, inventory, payment(s).
- expense to review: contains repair(s), maintenance, supplies, tools, computer, software, equipment, furniture, improvement(s), the word auto, vehicle(s) or truck(s); AND none of: rental, the word "rent", the word "lease" (not "leasehold"), fuel, insurance, the words loan(s), payable, interest, words starting gain, income, revenue.
- anything else: other (ignored).
The accountant can change any account's role on screen (step 2); then everything is worked out again.

THE RULES (in this order)
Put every line of every account in one list, in file order, each with its account and role.
A. Fixed asset lines:
 1. Transfers: a credit in one fixed asset account and a debit of the same amount in another fixed asset account, with the same num (not blank) and the same date. Neither is an addition or a disposal. Pair each credit with the first unused debit that fits.
 2. Reversals: of the lines left, a credit and a debit of the same amount in the same account, same name (ignoring case), at most 31 days apart. Pair each credit with the first unused debit that fits. Neither counts.
 3. Payments: of the debits left, in one account, 3 or more with the same name (not blank) and the same amount: likely loan payments. They are not additions.
 4. Additions: the other debits. Flag: journal (type contains "journal"); trade-in (memo contains "trade", "allowance" or "net of"); land (its account's name contains the word "land" but not "improvement"; land is not depreciated).
 5. The other credits, each one of three kinds: "return" if the type contains "credit" or "refund" and not "journal" (it reduces a purchase's cost); "recorded" if it has a num and some line with the same num and date either debits an accumulated depreciation account or is in an account whose name contains gain, loss, sale or disposal (the sale was booked; check it); otherwise "proceeds" (money received for an asset was posted to the asset, so no gain or loss was recorded).
B. Bills in expense-to-review accounts:
 1. Group lines into bills: lines with the same date, type, num and name (across all review accounts) when num is not blank; when num is blank, lines with the same account, date, type and name. A bill's total is the sum of its lines; keep its accounts in order and its first line's position in the list.
 2. Bills with a negative total (credits) are applied first, oldest first (ties: earlier in the list):
    - If the credit has a num and some fixed asset account has a debit with the same num and date, it is a reclass: among the positive bills that are over the threshold and share an account with it, remove (set to zero) one whose total equals the credit exactly; if none, the first set of them whose totals add up exactly to it (only when there are 14 such bills or fewer; try the sets in binary-counter order: number the bills 0, 1, 2 ... in date order, and for k = 1, 2, 3 ... the set holds bill i when bit i of k is 1).
    - Otherwise, if it has a name: take the latest bill (positive, same name ignoring case, sharing an account, dated on or before it) and reduce its total by the credit.
 3. A bill whose total is now MORE than the threshold is a bill to decide (threshold $2,500.00 unless she types another). Order them by date, then position. Each starts undecided; she chooses Capitalize or Keep as expense. A bill "repeats" (likely a service contract) when its name has 3 or more bills to decide in the same first account and those bills are all the same amount, or their memos, taken together, contain contract, maintenance, service, subscription, monthly, quarterly or annual. Repeating bills are still listed, with a note.
C. Possible sales elsewhere: credits in "other" accounts whose memo or name contains the word "sold", "sale of", "trade-in" (or "tradein") or "insurance proceeds" (any case), unless a "recorded" credit has the same num and date.
D. Depreciation booked = the sum of the lines in depreciation expense accounts. Cost opening = the sum of the fixed asset accounts' openings; accumulated depreciation opening = minus the sum of the accumulated depreciation accounts' openings (shown positive).
E. Mid-quarter: depreciable additions are the additions that are not land. The last three months start on the first day of the month two months before the period's last month (if the period is unknown: December 31 of the year of the latest line). If more than 40% of the depreciable additions (by amount) are dated on or after that day, flag it.
F. Figures she types (step 3d), each optional: last year's schedule total cost and total accumulated depreciation, and this year's depreciation. Opening differences = books' opening minus what she typed. Depreciation adjustment = typed this year's depreciation minus booked (positive: Dr Depreciation expense, Cr Accumulated depreciation; negative: the reverse). Something that is not a number shows "Not a number. Type digits, like 12,345.67." next to the box, and the old value is kept.
G. For each "proceeds" credit she types three figures: the asset's original cost and its accumulated depreciation at the end of last year (both from last year's schedule), and its depreciation this year up to the sale (from this year's depreciation report; empty means 0). Depreciation to date = the last two added. Gain = money received - (cost - depreciation to date); a negative gain is a loss. Once the first two are typed, the sale is settled.
H. Each bill marked Capitalize goes to a fixed asset account she picks (default: the first fixed asset account in the file), and each decided bill can carry a reason she picks: New equipment; Improvement or restoration; Repair or maintenance; De minimis: items $2,500 or less; Service contract or subscription; Other (see notes).
I. Balances after the proposed entries: cost after = the books' ending cost + bills marked Capitalize + for each settled sale (money received - its cost); accumulated depreciation after (shown positive) = the books' ending accumulated depreciation + the depreciation adjustment (if this year's depreciation was typed) - each settled sale's depreciation to date.

MESSAGES (code, level), only when they apply. When the file is not a general ledger: status NOT_RECOGNIZED and exactly one message, NOT_RECOGNIZED (stop), with the text above; nothing else in the report is needed. Level "stop" shows in a red box at the top; "care" and "info" in a list "Check these first", care first, labelled "Decide." and "For your file.". Each message names the step where she acts.
- UNREAD_ROWS (stop): rows with an amount but no readable date, or before any account; they are left out.
- FILE_DOES_NOT_ADD_UP (stop): names the accounts; a line is missing or changed; export again and do not edit it.
- NO_FIXED_ASSET_ACCOUNTS (care): no account recognized as a fixed asset; choose one in step 2.
- FA_CREDIT_BALANCE (care): a fixed asset account has a credit opening or ending; it may be a loan; check it in step 2.
- CAPITALIZE_CANDIDATES (care): N bills over the threshold were expensed; decide each in step 3b.
- ROUTINE_CHARGES (info): some bills repeat; usually a service contract.
- DISPOSALS (care): "N credit(s) to fixed asset accounts look(s) like money received for an asset ..." (singular or plural to match); type its cost and depreciation in step 3c.
- AD_NOT_REMOVED (care): there is a "proceeds" credit and no accumulated depreciation account has any debit line this year.
- DISPOSALS_RECORDED (info): a sale was booked with its depreciation or a gain or loss; check it and take it off the schedule.
- RETURNS (info): vendor credits to asset accounts reduce the cost; not sales.
- TRANSFERS (info): cost moved between asset accounts; not a purchase or a sale.
- REVERSALS (info): purchases entered and reversed; left out.
- LIKELY_LOAN_PAYMENTS (care): equal repeated payments posted to an asset account are usually loan payments; record the asset at full price and the loan as a liability.
- TRADE_IN (care): record the new asset at its full price; the traded-in asset is a sale (since 2018 trade-ins of equipment and vehicles are not like-kind exchanges) and may bring depreciation recapture.
- LAND (info): land is not depreciated; if a building came with it, split the price.
- JOURNAL_ENTRY_ADDITIONS (info): additions made by journal entry; for a reclass, the placed-in-service date is the original bill's.
- POSSIBLE_SALES (care): credits elsewhere mention a sale; an asset sold must come off the schedule and the books.
- AMORTIZATION (info): a depreciation expense account's name contains "amortization"; type depreciation and amortization together in step 3d.
- NO_DEPRECIATION_BOOKED (care): booked is 0 and (cost opening > 0 or there are additions).
- DEPRECIATION_DIFFERS (care): this year's depreciation typed and different from booked; says by how much and whether booked is less or more.
- OPENING_DIFFERS (care): either opening difference is not zero; says by how much, more or less in the books.
- MID_QUARTER (care): the mid-quarter convention may apply; check placed-in-service dates.
- PERIOD_NOT_A_YEAR (care): the period found is not exactly one year (from a date to the day before the same date a year later).
- PERIOD_UNKNOWN (info): the file does not say its dates; give the first and last line dates.
Status: NOT_RECOGNIZED as above, otherwise COMPUTED.

THE SCREEN
A step bar stays at the top while scrolling, with four steps: "1 Give the ledger", "2 Check the accounts" (you check), "3 Decide what was found" (you decide), "4 Print the workpaper" (built from your choices). The step in view is highlighted; once the file is read, steps 2 to 4 are links to their sections and step 1 starts over (after asking "Start over? Your decisions and the figures you typed for this file will be cleared."). A step gets a tick only when it is really done: step 2 after she presses the accounts button, step 3 when every bill is decided and every "proceeds" credit has its cost and depreciation typed. Section headings stop below the step bar when jumped to (scroll margin). On a phone the step bar is one compact row: numbers only, except the current step.
A line at the top of the workpaper says "You are looking at step N of 4." and then either "Still to do: step 2 (press "The accounts are right"); step 3 (N bills to decide, a sale's figures to type)." or "Everything is decided: print the workpaper in step 4."
Step 1, the start screen: the line "Step 1 of 4: give the page the client's general ledger for the year."; the title "What goes on the asset schedule?"; one sentence on what it does; a large drop box (a label wrapping a hidden <input type="file" id="file" accept=".csv,.txt,.xlsx,.xls,.xlsm">, also accepting drag and drop anywhere) "Drop the general ledger here, or click here to choose the file. Excel or CSV."; a hidden <div id="problem" role="alert"> for refusals and NOT_RECOGNIZED messages; a link that runs a small built-in made-up sample. Then "What file to ask the client for": the general ledger for the client's whole year, accrual basis, every account including those with no activity (turn off any option that hides them), one sheet, nothing deleted, sorted or retyped; how to export it from QuickBooks Online (Reports, General Ledger, dates, Accounting method Accrual, Run report, Export to Excel), QuickBooks Desktop (Reports, Accountant & Taxes, General Ledger, dates, Excel), Xero (Reports, Account Transactions, dates, all accounts, Update, Export, Excel), and other bookkeeping software (the report that lists every transaction by account, often called General Ledger, Account Transactions or Transaction Detail by Account, with the columns shown); a small example of the first rows, shown open. Then "What happens next" numbered 2 to 4, saying which parts are hers. Then "Where your data goes: nowhere" and "The page finds; you decide." Footer "Version 1.0.0."
Once a file is read, the start screen is replaced by the workpaper:
- A line saying which step she is on and what to do (it follows the step in view). The title, the layout, the period, the file name. Boxes for Client (filled with the company, full width), Workpaper ref., Prepared by, Prepared on (filled with today's date), Reviewed by, Reviewed on.
- <div id="verdict">: while anything is open, "[Company]: $X recorded as assets this year[; $Y more found in expense accounts for you to decide][; N sales or write-offs to settle]." where X is the depreciable additions, Y the total of the bills to decide, N the "proceeds" credits; under it "Decided D of B bills. To add to the depreciation schedule so far: $Z. Depreciation booked this year: $W." where Z = depreciable additions + bills marked Capitalize. Once every bill is decided and every sale settled (and there was at least one of either): "[Company]: $Z to add to the depreciation schedule[; N asset(s) to take off]." and under it "Recorded as assets: $X. From expense accounts: capitalized $A, kept as expense $B. [Each sale: gain or loss $G.] Depreciation booked this year: $W[, to adjust by $D]."
- <div id="stop-banner">: every stop message, each starting "Stop."; give it the hidden attribute when there are none.
- "Check these first": the care and info messages.
- Step 2, "Check the accounts" (you check): "What this is for / What to do" in two sentences. A table: account, opening and ending (as $1,234.56 Dr or Cr), number of lines, and a <select class="role" data-account="FULL NAME"> with the options fa "Fixed asset (cost)", ad "Accumulated depreciation", dep "Depreciation expense", review "Expense: check for purchases", other "Other: the page ignores it". Changing one reworks everything. Then a button id="accounts-ok": "The accounts are right: go to step 3".
- Step 3, "Decide what was found", with a "What this is for / What to do" box, in four parts, each labelled with who acts:
  3a "Bought this year and recorded as assets" (you check): a note "Found automatically in the fixed asset accounts." followed by "N lines have notes to check." when any addition is flagged, or "Check that each is a purchase." when none is; the additions (date, account, from, description and num, cost, with notes for journal entry, trade-in and land) and a total; then lines for left-out loan payments, transfers and reversals.
  3b "Bills in expense accounts that may be equipment" (you decide): a short explanation (de minimis safe harbor: items of $2,500 or less per invoice or per item, $5,000 with an applicable financial statement such as audited statements, if expensed in the books and elected on each year's return; a bill over the limit can hold items under it; a repair that keeps something running stays an expense, one that betters, restores or adapts it is capitalized; subscriptions and services are expenses). A box id="threshold" "List bills over" (default 2500.00) with a button id="update-threshold" "Apply". A count "N of M not decided yet.". A table of the bills: date, accounts, from, description (with "repeats: likely a service contract" when it repeats, and for a bill of several lines, each account's part and the line amounts, "Check each item against the limit."), amount, and two radio buttons <input type="radio" class="dec" data-id="BILL ID" value="cap"> "Capitalize" and value="exp" "Keep as expense", none checked at first. The bill id is "c" followed by its first line's position. Under a bill marked Capitalize, "to" <select class="target" data-id="BILL ID"> listing the fixed asset accounts; under any decided bill, "why" <select class="reason" data-id="BILL ID"> with the reasons in rule H and an empty "(choose)". Choosing reworks everything.
  3c "Sold, traded in, returned or written off" (you decide): an explanation (ask the client which asset; type its cost and accumulated depreciation at the end of last year from last year's schedule, and its depreciation this year up to the sale from this year's report; if this year's figure in 3d comes from the tax software it already includes this asset's depreciation for the months it was owned). For "proceeds" credits a table with date, account, description, money received, three boxes <input class="disp" data-id="SALE ID" data-f="cost|ad|ady"> (in that order; the sale id is "d" followed by the credit's position in the list of all lines), and the gain or loss (or "type the cost and last year's depreciation"). Work it out when the focus leaves all of the sale boxes (moving from one sale box to another, of any sale, must not redraw the page, or what she types next is lost); also a button id="update-disp" "Work out the gain or loss". Then a line for each "recorded" credit, each "return", and each possible sale elsewhere.
  3d "Does it agree?" (you decide): boxes id="sched-cost" (last year's schedule: total cost), id="sched-ad" (last year's schedule: accumulated depreciation), id="tax-dep" (this year's depreciation), with the explanation: this year's figure is the depreciation the books should carry; for books on the tax basis, the tax depreciation including bonus and section 179 (for an S corporation or partnership, add the section 179 stated separately); for GAAP statements, book depreciation. A button id="update" "Compare". These three boxes are read only when she presses Compare: typing in them or moving between them must not redraw the page (that would lose what she typed). A table: check, in the books, you typed, result ("agrees", or "books are $D higher/lower than ...").
- Step 4, "The workpaper" (built from your choices): a main button id="print" "Print or save as PDF" (window.print()) and a link "Start over with another file". If anything is undecided or a "proceeds" credit has no figures, a red box "Not finished: ..." saying it is left out below. Then: "Add to the depreciation schedule" (depreciable additions and bills marked Capitalize, by date: placed in service (confirm), asset, from, in the books as, cost; a total; a note that the bill date is not always the placed-in-service date and that method, life, bonus and section 179 are chosen in the tax software); land not depreciated; "Take off the schedule (confirm with the client)"; returns that reduce cost; "Proposed entries" as a journal table id="entries" (entry, account, debit, credit), numbered AJE 1, AJE 2 ..., each followed by a line of explanation: for bills marked Capitalize, one entry per pair of chosen fixed asset account and expense account, "Dr [chosen account] / Cr [expense account]" with the items named; for each settled sale, "Dr Accumulated depreciation [depreciation to date]; Dr [asset account] [money received] (undo the credit); Cr [asset account] [original cost]; Cr Gain on sale of assets [gain] (or Dr Loss on sale of assets [loss])"; the depreciation adjustment, "Dr Depreciation expense / Cr Accumulated depreciation" (or the reverse). Below the table, as a list: for loan payments, record the asset at full price and the loan; for opening differences, find what changed before posting. Under the roll-forward, when there are entries: "After the proposed entries: cost $C; accumulated depreciation $A." (rule I), and that these should agree with the schedule's totals at the end of this year once its additions and disposals are entered. "Questions for the client" (each bill, each credit, each possible sale, and for each addition when it was put into use and whether it is new or used, adding the gross vehicle weight rating (over 6,000 lb?) and business-use percentage for vehicles). The cost roll-forward (account, opening, debits, credits, ending, total) and the accumulated depreciation roll-forward (opening, added, removed, ending, shown positive). "What I read": layout, number of accounts and lines, and whether every account adds up. Footer: "Made by What goes on the asset schedule? version 1.0.0, on this computer. The file was read here and not sent anywhere. Arithmetic is done in whole cents. This is a workpaper for review: the page finds; you decide what to capitalize, how to depreciate and what to post."
- Printing shows only the heading, the verdict and step 4, plus the checks, each bill with its decision ("capitalize", "keep as expense" or "NOT DECIDED", with the reason) and the accounts as checked; it hides the step bar, steps 2 and 3, the buttons, the "you decide" labels and focus outlines, keeps headings with what follows, and replaces the title with "Fixed asset review, year ended [period end]". Pressing Print while something is not finished first asks "This workpaper is not finished: ... Print anyway?".
Whenever she changes a role or a decision, presses Apply, Compare or "Work out the gain or loss", or leaves the sale boxes, review the file again with everything she has entered so far, redraw, and keep her place on the page and what she typed in the header boxes.

THE REPORT OBJECT (window.__report; money in dollars as numbers)
version "1.0.0", file, status, exceptions [{code, level, message}], layout, company, period {from, to} as "YYYY-MM-DD" or null, threshold, accounts {full name: role}, rows (number of lines), notAddUp [names], rollforward [{account, opening, debits (all debit lines), credits (all credit lines, negative), ending}] for fixed asset accounts, adRollforward [{account, opening, credits, debits, ending}] (signed, debit positive), additions [{account, date, num, name, memo, amount, journal, tradeIn, land}], disposals [{account, date, num, name, memo, amount (positive), kind, id, and for settled sales: cost, adPrior, adThisYear, adToDate, gain}], transfers [{from, to, date, amount (positive)}], reversals [{account, amount (positive), name}], payments [{account, name, count, amount}], candidates [{id, account (first), accounts, parts [{account, amount}], date, num, name, memo, amount, lines, routine, decision ("undecided", "cap" or "exp"), target, reason}], possibleSales [{account, date, name, memo, amount (positive)}], costOpening, adOpening (positive), costEnding, adEnding (positive), additionsTotal, scheduleAdditions (additions that are not land), candidatesTotal, capitalizeTotal, undecided (count), depreciationBooked, faAccounts (names), costAfter, adAfter, and when typed: taxDepreciation, depreciationAdjustment, scheduleCost, scheduleAD, openingDiffCost, openingDiffAD.

What it doesn't do

  • It does not depreciate anything. The method, life, bonus and section 179 stay in your tax software.
  • It does not see inside a bill. A bill over $2,500 can hold items under the de minimis limit, so check the invoice before you capitalize.
  • It does not know what the client did with an asset. A credit to an asset account could be a sale, a trade-in, an insurance payout or a correction. The questions for the client ask.
  • It does not handle everything on the balance sheet. Leases, construction in progress and intangibles are out of scope. So is splitting a building's price between land and building.
  • It has not met real client exports yet. It was tested on files built from QuickBooks' and Xero's published report layouts. If your export doesn't read, tell me and I will add the layout.
